images.filename: Inside the Tomb of the Eagles - geograph.org.uk - 882949.jpg
images.caption: Inside the Tomb of the Eagles This Chambered Cairn is estimated to have been built around 3000bc, and used for approximately 800 years. It is 3.5 metres high and consists of a rectangular main chamber, divided into stalls and side cells. It is believed the human remains belonged to around 340 individuals. No complete skeleton was found suggesting that the bodies had been excarnated - left outside until the bones were clean. Recent research questions both the excarnation idea and number of people in the tomb. Once inside the Tomb, at some point the skulls were laid in side chambers and the other bones set in the two end cells.

images.filename: The Tomb of the Eagles - geograph.org.uk - 1452411.jpg
images.caption: The Tomb of the Eagles This neolithic burial chamber was found by a farmer when the stones were uncovered following a storm. His family still owns the land and access is via a visitor centre at South Liddel. The 5,000 year old cairn gets its name from the talons of sea eagles that were found with the human remains - they may have been hunting trophies but if so it is not known what methods were used to hunt such fearsome creatures. It is possible to enter the chamber using a narrow entrance close to where the visitors are standing.
